title: What is the principle of least privilege, and how do you scope a policy to a single resource (e.g. grant access to only one S3 bucket or one ECR repository)?
shortTitle: Principle of Least Privilege and Scoping a Policy to One Resource

s1_definition.profdef: The principle of least privilege states that every identity should have exactly the permissions it needs to do its job and nothing more. In IAM you apply it by scoping policies tightly: naming the specific actions, the specific resource ARNs, and often condition keys, rather than using wildcards. Scoping to a single resource means setting the policy's `Resource` element to that one resource's ARN — for example one S3 bucket's objects or one ECR repository — so the identity cannot touch any other.
s1_definition.analogy: At National Bank of India, least privilege means Rajesh the teller gets a key that opens only his own cash drawer, not the vault, not the manager's office, and not every other teller's drawer. If someone steals his key, the damage is limited to that one drawer. Giving him a master key "just in case" would be convenient but reckless. In IAM, the one-drawer key is a policy whose Resource names exactly one bucket.
s1_definition.oneliner: Grant only the exact actions on the exact resource that the job needs, so a leak or mistake can only harm that one thing.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The principle of least privilege states that every identity should have exactly the permissions it needs to do its job and nothing more. In IAM you apply it by scoping policies tightly: naming the specific actions, the specific resource ARNs, and often condition keys, rather than using wildcards. Scoping to a single resource means setting the policy's `Resource` element to that one resource's ARN — for example one S3 bucket's objects or one ECR repository — so the identity cannot touch any other.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At National Bank of India, least privilege means Rajesh the teller gets a key that opens only his own cash drawer, not the vault, not the manager's office, and not every other teller's drawer. If someone steals his key, the damage is limited to that one drawer. Giving him a master key "just in case" would be convenient but reckless. In IAM, the one-drawer key is a policy whose Resource names exactly one bucket.

**One line to remember:** Grant only the exact actions on the exact resource that the job needs, so a leak or mistake can only harm that one thing.

sections.s2_technical:
Least privilege reduces blast radius. If a service's credentials leak, an attacker can only do what that narrow policy allows. The opposite — a policy with `"Action": "*"` and `"Resource": "*"` — means a single leak compromises the entire account. In a bank that difference is the difference between a contained incident and a front-page breach.

Scoping to a single S3 bucket requires two statements, because bucket-level operations and object-level operations use different ARN shapes. Listing the bucket needs the bucket ARN itself, while reading objects needs the ARN with a `/*` suffix.

```json
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Sid": "ListOnlyThisBucket",
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": "s3:ListBucket",
      "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::nbi-customer-statements"
    },
    {
      "Sid": "ReadObjectsInThisBucket",
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": ["s3:GetObject", "s3:PutObject"],
      "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::nbi-customer-statements/*"
    }
  ]
}
```

Scoping to a single ECR repository follows the same idea. You name the repository ARN so the service can pull only its own container image, not every image in the account:

```json
{
  "Effect": "Allow",
  "Action": ["ecr:GetDownloadUrlForLayer", "ecr:BatchGetImage"],
  "Resource": "arn:aws:ecr:ap-south-1:123456789012:repository/settlement-service"
}
```

You can tighten even further with condition keys. For example, restrict access to objects with a specific prefix, or require that requests come over TLS, or require multi-factor authentication for deletes. In code you rarely write policies at runtime; you attach them to the Role the service assumes, and the SDK simply inherits whatever that Role permits.

A senior nuance: achieving least privilege is iterative. You start restrictive, run the workload, read IAM Access Analyzer findings and CloudTrail denied-action logs, and add only the permissions the workload actually used. AWS also offers Access Analyzer policy generation that drafts a least-privilege policy from observed activity.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The settlement service only ever touches one bucket, `nbi-customer-statements`, and one container repository, `settlement-service`. If we give it account-wide S3 and ECR access, a compromise of this one service exposes every bucket and image in the bank. This is exactly what resource-scoped policies solve: name the one bucket and the one repository, and nothing else is reachable.

Problem 2 — The service must list and read and write statements but has no reason to read any other team's bucket. This is exactly what the two-statement bucket scoping provides, separating the list permission on the bucket from the object permissions inside it.

We will build a `PolicyScopeValidator` that checks whether a requested action and resource are inside the allowed scope, modelling the deny-by-default behaviour. Classes: `ScopedPolicy`, `PolicyScopeValidator`, and a demo proving that in-scope requests pass and out-of-scope requests fail.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a scoped policy naming exactly one bucket (list and object) and one ECR repository, with a fixed set of allowed actions.

Step 1 — The service asks to GetObject on `nbi-customer-statements/stmt1.pdf`. The validator checks the action is in the allowed set (it is) and the resource matches the `nbi-customer-statements/*` pattern (it does), so the result is allowed.

Step 2 — The service asks to BatchGetImage on its own ECR repository. The action is allowed and the resource matches the repository ARN exactly, so it is allowed to pull its own image.

Step 3 — The service asks to GetObject on `nbi-payroll-secret/salaries.csv`. The action is allowed, but the resource does not match any allowed ARN, so the result is denied. This is least privilege containing the blast radius: even if this service were compromised, it cannot read the payroll bucket.

Step 4 — The service asks to DeleteObject on a statement. The action `s3:DeleteObject` is not in the allowed set at all, so it is denied, proving the service can read and write but never delete.

```
2026-10-29 00:52:14 [INFO] Read own statement:  true
2026-10-29 00:52:14 [INFO] Pull own image:      true
2026-10-29 00:52:14 [WARNING] Read OTHER bucket:   false
2026-10-29 00:52:14 [WARNING] Delete (not granted):false
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Request: action + resource
    │
    ▼
  PolicyScopeValidator.allowed(policy, action, resource)
    │
    ├─ action in allowed set? ── no ──→ DENY
    │        yes
    ├─ resource matches a scoped ARN? ── no ──→ DENY
    │        yes
    ▼
  ALLOW (only own bucket + own repo reachable)

  own-bucket GetObject ─────────→ ALLOW
  own-repo  BatchGetImage ──────→ ALLOW
  payroll-bucket GetObject ─────→ DENY (out of scope)
  DeleteObject ─────────────────→ DENY (action not granted)
```
sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Scope Validation ═══

  ┌─ Patterns ─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Specification: action-spec AND resource-spec must hold  │
  │   WHY: both must match for least privilege              │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID ────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ S: ScopedPolicy holds scope; Validator only decides      │
  │ I: action check and resource check are separate concerns │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Class Diagram ──────────────────────────────────────────
  ┌───────────────────────┐        ┌────────────────────────┐
  │ ScopedPolicy          │◀───────│ PolicyScopeValidator    │
  │ - allowedActions:Set  │  uses  │ + allowed(p,act,res)    │
  │ - allowedResources:[] │        └────────────────────────┘
  │ + actionAllowed(a)    │
  │ + resourceAllowed(r)  │
  └───────────────────────┘

  Contract for allowed(policy, action, resource):
    Pre:  policy non-null
    Post: true only if action in set AND resource matches a scoped ARN
    Default: false (deny by default)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The principle of least privilege means every identity gets exactly the permissions it needs to do its job and not one permission more. The whole point is to shrink the blast radius: if a service's credentials leak or a bug misbehaves, the damage is limited to the narrow set of actions and resources that identity was granted, instead of the entire account. The opposite — a policy with action star and resource star — turns a single leaked token into a full account compromise, which in a bank is catastrophic.

The way you achieve it in IAM is by scoping tightly on three dimensions: name the specific actions, name the specific resource ARNs, and where it helps add condition keys. Scoping to a single S3 bucket actually needs two statements because bucket-level and object-level operations use different ARN shapes — listing the bucket uses the bucket ARN itself, while reading and writing objects uses the bucket ARN with a slash-star suffix. Scoping to a single ECR repository is the same idea: you put the one repository ARN in the resource element so the service can pull only its own image and no other.

At National Bank of India our settlement service only ever touches one bucket and one container repository. So its Role carries a policy that names exactly that bucket for list, get, and put, and exactly that repository for image pulls, and nothing else. The result is that even if the service were fully compromised, an attacker could not read the payroll bucket or any other team's data, and could not delete a statement because the delete action was never granted. That containment is the entire value of least privilege.

One senior point I always make is that least privilege is iterative, not a one-shot guess. I start deliberately restrictive, run the workload, then read IAM Access Analyzer findings and CloudTrail logs of denied actions, and add back only the permissions the workload genuinely used. AWS even has Access Analyzer policy generation that drafts a least-privilege policy from observed activity. That evidence-based tightening is how you end up with a policy that is both secure and actually works in production.
